title: Comments of EDF Power Solutions, Inc. in response to the 60-Day Compliance Filing by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. on 02/23/2026 under ER26-1479.

documents.name: Comments of EDFps in ER26-1479.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                             Docket No. ER26-1479-000


                       COMMENTS OF EDF POWER SOLUTIONS, INC.

          Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission or FERC),1 EDF power solutions, Inc. (EDFps)

respectfully submits these comments in response to the 60-Day Compliance Filing2 filed by PJM

Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) on February 23, 2026 (PJM Compliance Filing). The PJM

Compliance Filing was submitted in response to the Commission’s December 18, 2025 Order on

Show Cause Proceeding,3 regarding the co-location of large loads in PJM.

I.        SUMMARY OF COMMENTS

          PJM’s proposed framework for new transmission services presents an important

opportunity to support the reliable and flexible integration of large load resources. PJM’s

proposed three new transmission service options will allow large loads to combine Firm and

Non-Firm Contract Demand services, facilitating flexible co-location arrangements and efficient

interconnection.

          PJM’s proposed 50 MW Retail Behind the Meter Generation (BTMG) threshold, on the

other hand, is arbitrary and too low. It will disincentivize large loads from installing their own

generation and thereby stifle innovation. The Retail BTMG threshold should instead be based on


1
    18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.213 (2025).
2
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 60-Day Compliance Filing for Co-Located Load Related to Revisions to
Open Access Transmission Tariff to Comply with Commission Order in Docket No. EL25-49, Feb. 23,
2026.
3
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (December 18 Order).
 percentage of the load size. EDFps suggests 100% of the load size, at the electrical location,

combined with operational safeguards and appropriate transmission charges. There are

significant benefits of BTMG co-location that should be encouraged. BTMG can reduce grid

congestion, avoid queue delays, lower network upgrade needs, and provide economic and

community benefits. EDFps suggests a “bifurcated netting” approach, which allows netting of

generation up to the Retail BTMG size while charging the full load for transmission service.

       Finally, PJM’s proposed BTMG changes require modifications to ensure that (1) a Retail

BTMG resource that exceeds the established threshold can still be netted up to the threshold

amount; and (2) a BTMG resource can continue to serve load (provide ride-through capacity)

during a grid curtailment event, similar to backup generation.

II.    BACKGROUND

       EDFps develops, builds, operates, and manages renewable energy projects throughout

North America, including in PJM, MISO, SPP, and ERCOT. As a market-leading independent

power producer and service provider for over 35 years, EDFps delivers grid-scale power,

including wind (onshore and offshore), solar photovoltaic, and storage projects; distribution-

scale power, including solar and storage; and asset optimization. The company also provides

technical, operational, and commercial expertise to maximize performance of generating

projects. EDFps is an active participant in interconnection and large load-related policy

discussions, rulemaking proceedings, and reform efforts.

       On February 23, 2026, PJM submitted the 60-Day Compliance Filing in response to the

Commission’s December 18 Order. Among other things, PJM proposes to adopt a revised

definition of Retail BTMG to include a new 50 MW materiality threshold and to establish three

new transmission service options for large loads.




                                                 2
 III.       COMMENTS

           A.          PJM’s Proposed 50 MW Materiality Threshold for New Retail BTMG is
                       Arbitrarily Too Low: The Threshold Should Vary Based on the Size of the
                       Load.

           PJM proposes a materiality threshold of up to 50 MW for a new generator at the same

electrical location as the Network Load to qualify for Retail BTMG.4 According to PJM, its

proposed 50 MW threshold corresponds with the PJM Board’s definition of large load additions,

which are individual loads of 50 MW or greater at a single point of interconnection.5 However,

the 50 MW Retail BTMG threshold is arbitrary and could disincentivize retail customers from

installing their own generation. The benefits of “bring your own generation” to the grid has been

recognized as an essential element of the drive to meet the demand of new large loads.6 To meet

this goal, the Retail BTMG threshold should be established based on 100% of the size of the

large load it serves at that electrical location, coupled with operational safeguards and a

requirement that the appropriate transmission service charges are paid.

           Large loads come in all sizes and co-location arrangements can vary significantly. The

Retail BTMG threshold should be flexible and non-discriminatory to account for these

differences. For example, with a 50 MW Retail BTMG threshold, a 50 MW large load could

theoretically cover 100% of its load with Retail BTMG. A large load of 200 MW, on the other

hand, could only cover 25% of its load with the 50 MW threshold. PJM’s proposed 50 MW

threshold will stifle innovation and arbitrarily incentivize the development of smaller loads rather

    PJM Compliance Filing at p. 6-7.
5
    Id. at p. 11-12.
6
 December 18 Order, Rosner concurring at P 8. See also Energy Secretary Encourages Data Centers to
Bring Their Own Generation, The Ohio Mfrs.’ Ass’n (Oct. 10, 2025), available at:
https://www.ohiomfg.com/our-communities/energy-secretary-encourages-data-centers-to-bring-their-
own-generation/; “Behind-the-Meter” AI Projects Surge in the U.S., Nam News Room (Feb. 6, 2026),
available at: https://nam.org/behind-the-meter-ai-projects-surge-in-u-s-35696/.


                                                    3
 than designing the loads to meet the needs of the large load customer. It may also incentivize

large loads to be segmented in close but separate electrical locations, resulting in inefficient and

redundant construction of interconnection facilities.

       The optimal sizing of Retail BTMG, such as solar plus battery energy storage systems

(BESS) or some other combination, to support an AI data center would most certainly exceed 50

MW. An arbitrary 50 MW limit will require that these new large loads develop new grid-

connected resources instead of BTMG resources. This would force new generation resources –

which are solely intended to serve new large loads – into the generation interconnection queue

with full wholesale interconnection studies that would otherwise be unnecessary. It may also

call for network upgrades that would also otherwise be unnecessary.

       Stripping the new large load with BTMG of netting rights penalizes the very co-located

configurations that can ease grid congestion. BTMG arrangements can benefit the transmission

system in many ways, such as by serving load on a streamlined basis, avoiding queue delays in

the generator interconnection process, and reducing the need for expensive grid upgrades.

BTMG co-locating with large loads can also reduce congestion costs and allow the load to

provide demand response services if the power demands are flexible. Finally, BTMG resources

will provide benefits to states and communities by facilitating new large load facilities that can

provide a host of benefits to local communities in the form of tax revenues, construction jobs,

and employment.

       EDFps understands that there could be impacts to operation of the transmission system if

the Retail BTMG is not available. This possibility can be managed to preserve the benefits of

BTMG to the new load and to the grid while also protecting the grid from negative impacts if the

BTMG is unavailable. For example, PJM could establish a “bifurcated netting” approach:




                                                  4
         •    If a Retail BTMG system exceeds 50 MW, the large load should still be permitted to

             net its generation against its load for the purposes of energy and capacity market

             settlements.

        •    To satisfy concerns regarding transmission cost shifting, PJM could establish a

             framework where facilities with BTMG that exceeds 50 MW pay transmission and/or

             distribution network charges without the benefit of netting (i.e., paying transmission

             and/or distribution charges based on the gross load or agreed-upon contract demand).

        This bifurcated netting approach is beneficial in that it preserves the economic incentive

to build various resources with storage configurations directly at the load center (such as large-

scale renewables plus storage, or natural gas resources plus storage). Setting the Retail BTMG

threshold at 100% of the load it serves at that electrical location is consistent with the

Commission’s “beneficiary pays” principle when it is coupled with transmission charges that

appropriately reflect the full loads potential usage of the transmission system.7

        B.      For Retail BTMG Resources that Exceed the Materiality Threshold Size,
                PJM Should Allow Netting Up to the Threshold Amount.

        PJM states that going forward any new large Retail BTMG that is greater than the

proposed threshold would not qualify as Retail BTMG and that “a Retail BTMG cannot both net

up to a certain threshold but still potentially have generation and load above that threshold which




7
 Under the “beneficiary pays” cost causation principle, rates must “reflect to some degree the costs
actually caused by the customer who must pay them.” Midwest ISO Transmission Owners v. FERC, 373
F.3d 1361, 1368 (D.C. Cir. 2004). Costs must be allocated in a manner that is at least roughly
commensurate with the benefits an entity receives. Ill. Com. Comm’n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 474-78
(7th Cir. 2009) (remanding Commission order for further proceedings in light of Commission’s failure to
provide substantial evidence supporting Commission’s approval of cost allocation method as complying
with “beneficiary pays” principle).


                                                   5
 cannot be netted.”8 PJM claims that this provision is consistent with its interpretation of the

Commission’s directive in the December 18 Order.9

            In the December 18 Order, the Commission found that PJM’s existing Retail BTMG

rules were no longer just and reasonable for use by large loads because large loads do not carry

reserves and such loads must nevertheless be served, which would allow them to “lean on the

PJM system when the co-located generation is on a full or partial outage or if the load exceeds

the rating of the co-located generation.”10

            PJM’s filing in response to the December 18 Order, however, makes significant changes

to the transmission service requirements that alleviate the ability of large loads with Retail

BTMG to lean on the system. PJM states that its proposed contract demand service (consisting

of Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service) provides “an alternative to NITS

for those Co-Located Loads willing and able to limit energy withdrawals from the Transmission

System.”11 PJM states that “there can be no ‘unstudied’ and/or ‘unknown’ portion of the Co-

Located Load that is not covered by either Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service or

dedicated generation from the Co-Located Generating Facility (as backed up by Non-Firm

Contract Demand Transmission Service).”12

            Thus, in the case of a Retail BTMG resource, the load being served would be required to

purchase Non-Firm Contract Demand up to the amount covered by the Retail BTMG and Firm

                                                   6
 Contract Demand for the remainder of the load. If the Retail BTMG was equal to the size of the

load and the load is fully covered by Non-Firm Contract Demand, the load would be limited to

taking energy “on an as-needed and as-available basis,”13 for its entire load and could not lean on

the system.

            PJM indicates that a “hybrid approach,” where a Retail BTMG can both net up to a

certain threshold and have generation and load above the threshold that cannot be netted, would

(1) impose significant metering costs all Retail BTMG that would have to install previously

unnecessary equipment; and (2) amplify compliance risks in monitoring and reporting different

generator and load thresholds.14

            PJM’s rejection of a hybrid approach is unwarranted. First, grandfathered Retail BTMG

would not face any additional metering costs, nor would entities that installed Retail BTMG that

did not exceed the threshold. Only entities choosing to install larger Retail BTMG resources

would have to install the appropriate metering. These entities can decide whether the costs and

compliance risks (if any) are cost-effective for their business. Rejecting a hybrid approach

altogether would discourage investment in BTMG.

            C.       Co-Located Retail BTMG Resources Must Be Permitted to Provide Ride-
                     Through Capacity During Curtailments.

            PJM proposes that the Retail BTMG threshold excludes backup generation “at the same

electrical location as the retail load that can only be used to serve such retail load during

conditions that may threaten the integrity or reliability of the PJM Region or the regional power

system.”15 EDFps interprets this to mean that backup generation can be used during a grid



13
     PJM Compliance Filing at p. 21.
14
     Id. at p. 11.
15
     Id. at p. 7.


                                                   7
 curtailment event. However, it is not clear whether the Retail BTMG itself can operate during a

grid curtailment event.

          Large loads electing to take “Interim NITS” accept the risk of grid curtailment but they

should not have to accept a complete operational downtime during a grid curtailment. Like

backup generation, discharging a BTMG BESS (or a BESS charged by BTM solar) directly to

the data center load during a grid curtailment event is a necessary self-supply function. The

Commission should direct PJM to explicitly clarify that BESS and hybrid systems functioning in

a load-following, non-exporting capacity manner during a curtailment event qualify under the

“backup generation” exemption, and can continue to serve the load, regardless of their size.

          D.       PJM’s Proposed Three New Transmission Services Should Be Accepted.

          EDFps supports PJM’s proposal to add three new transmission service options to benefit

large load customers. According to PJM, large load customers will have the option to take a

combination of Firm and Non-Firm Contract Demand service as long as the combined service

fully covers the co-located loads total load.16 The Non-Firm Contract Demand service provides

a useful option for large loads that do not necessarily intend to withdraw energy from the grid on

a regular basis and instead plan to rely on Retail BTMG for all or a portion of its load.

          The new transmission service options will encourage flexible co-location structures that

will enable speedy and reliable interconnection for large loads. Standardized yet flexible rules to

accommodate different co-location structures with varying operational needs and capabilities are

needed to meet the challenges of serving the power needs of new large loads.




16
     PJM Brief at p. 11.


                                                  8
 IV.    CONCLUSION

       PJM’s proposed framework for Retail BTMG thresholds and new transmission service

options presents an important opportunity to support the reliable and flexible integration of large

load resources. To ensure the effectiveness and fairness of these proposals, PJM should (1) set a

Retail BTMG materiality threshold that is based on 100% of the load; (2) allow a hybrid

approach to netting of Retail BTMG resources that exceed the threshold; and (3) expressly

permit co-located Retail BTMG and backup generation—including BESS and hybrid systems—

to operate during grid curtailment events. These clarifications will preserve incentives for

investment in innovative on-site generation and storage, enhance reliability, and provide large

load customers with the operational flexibility they require. Adoption of the three new

transmission service options will further promote efficient interconnection and accommodate the

evolving needs of large energy users. For these reasons, the Commission should approve PJM’s

proposed changes, with the recommended modifications/clarifications.
